title: Winning is Futile
author: Moore, Brandon
summary: Brandon Moore argues that winning—as commonly understood through status, wealth, and ease—fails to build grit in young men because it requires no encounter with struggle. True success is formed not by winning but by discipline learned through loss and hard work. Fathers, Moore insists, bear a unique and irreplaceable responsibility for this formation: inviting sons into their own labors, sharing stories of their own youth, and modeling what it looks like to keep working without a clear reason. The right competitor for a son is not his peers but an ever-improving version of himself—with Christ's perfection as the horizon that gives the pursuit its shape. Fathers who intentionally teach their sons to work hard and persevere are, Moore concludes, the ones who change the world one family at a time.
points: Winning, without the experience of struggle, cannot teach grit. The virtues that produce lasting success—discipline, perseverance, the refusal to quit—are formed in loss and hard labor, not in achievement. A man who has only won does not know what he is made of.

Fathers are uniquely positioned to transmit the ethic of work. No institution replaces the father who stacks wood with his son for no obvious reason and lets the boy feel the aches that accompany building real strength—and who shares the story of how he himself learned to work.

The right competitor for a young man is himself. Rather than training sons to outperform peers, fathers should help sons pursue an ever-growing version of themselves, pointing them toward the standard of Christ's excellence as the horizon that gives the pursuit its inexhaustible shape.
quotes: Winning does not teach a man grit. It's the losing, the struggle, the refusal to quit that provides this education.
Stack wood with him, just for the sake of doing it. It will drive him mad because he won't understand why you would do this to yourself. Just grin and continue working.

Hard work will build the character that outlasts the competition provided by his peers. Help him craft the only man worthy of his competition, himself. That is to say, the ever growing and learning version of himself.

Jesus is perfect excellence. You are correct to recoil at the blasphemy that someone could dare achieve the perfection that is Christ. It cannot be done, but we are still called to try. We are meant to strive towards it with every breath of our being.
What you can do, is become one of the fathers intentionally teaching and training his sons to be better men than he is. That, my friend, is how we truly win.
